questions.q: At which stage of the request lifecycle does queuing delay first get introduced?
options: Tokenization
Routing and admission, when a GPU is already busy
Detokenization and response streaming
GPU execution (the forward pass)
questions.explain: Queuing delay happens at the routing/admission stage: if every GPU replica is already busy, a request waits here before any model code runs at all.

questions.q: Why can a model-only micro-benchmark look much faster than what users actually experience in production?
options: Micro-benchmarks use a different, more accurate clock
It only measures the GPU execution stage, missing queuing delay, cold starts, and batch-formation wait
Production servers always use slower GPUs than benchmarks
Tokenization time is impossible to measure
questions.explain: A benchmark of the forward pass alone omits queuing delay, cold starts, and batch-formation wait — stages that often dominate real-world latency.

questions.q: What is a "cold start" in the context of model serving?
options: A request that arrives with no prompt text
The delay from loading a model's weights into GPU memory before it can serve its first request
A request that gets rejected by the load balancer
The time it takes to tokenize a very long prompt
questions.explain: A cold start is the delay a new replica incurs loading model weights into GPU memory, which can take anywhere from seconds to a couple of minutes for a large model.

questions.q: What is the key difference between the serving framework's job and the model runtime's job?
options: There is no difference — they are the same layer
The serving framework handles routing, admission, scheduling, and the client protocol; the runtime executes the actual GPU forward pass
The runtime handles networking; the framework handles only tokenization
The framework only runs on CPU, while the runtime only runs on GPU
questions.explain: The serving framework (like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, or Triton) owns the request-handling layers, while the underlying runtime owns the actual matrix-multiplication execution on the GPU.

questions.q: Why might a scheduler deliberately hold a request for a few extra milliseconds before running it?
options: To intentionally punish slow clients
Because tokenization requires extra time for every request
To give dynamic batching a chance to group it with other incoming requests, trading a little latency for better throughput
Because GPUs cannot process one request at a time
questions.explain: This is the batch-formation wait: a scheduler doing dynamic batching may hold a request briefly, hoping another request arrives to batch with it, improving overall throughput at a small latency cost.
